newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian miners launch charge against power levy.
newsitem.headline: Australian miners launch charge against power levy.

text.p: A quiet war has erupted between minerals and energy producers and the government of Australia's most populated state over the planned imposition of a A$100 million a year electricity levy.

The levy, announced in the New South Wales (NSW) state budget of June 10, had attracted little attention as a noisy debate swirled over the government's decision to introduce a 10 percent bed tax for Sydney hotels.
The bed tax would raise only about 65 percent of annual revenue which the electricity levy aims to produce.
But the bed tax has grabbed headlines because of claims it would jeopardise Sydney's 2000 Olympics.
Minerals producers, meanwhile, have been fighting behind the scenes to contain potential blow-outs in the power levy.
Denis Porter, deputy executive director of the NSW Minerals Council, told Reuters his organisation had written several times to the government over the electricity levy "without success".
Now it was attempting to have state Treasurer Michael Egan agree to cap the levy at A$100 million, he said.
Industries which would be particularly hit by the levy include coal mining, aluminium smelting and petroleum refining.

Their profits would be cut and expansion in NSW prejudiced, the Minerals Council said. "The tax is a major blow to New South Wales coal and mineral exporters," executive director Jane Robertson said in a statement.
The tax would impose an average cost of five cents to 12 cents per tonne of coal produced. This would be added directly to the cost of producing coal, Porter said.
"This is a significant cost given the extremely competitive markets within which our industry operates," Robertson said.
NSW, Australia's second largest coal state after Queensland, produces most of the country's semi-soft and steaming coal.
The Tomago aluminium smelter near Newcastle is another heavy electricity user which will be hit hard by the levy.
Tomago, which is expanding annaul capacity by 10 percent to 440,000 tonnes by early 1999, is owned 36.05 percent by Gove Aluminium Ltd, which is turn is owned 70 percent by CSR Ltd.
Tomago is also owned 36.05 percent by France's Pechiney SA, 12.4 percent by Germany's VAW Aluminium AG and 15.5 percent by life insurer Australian Mutual Provident Society.

Electricity costs at the Ampol refinery at Kurnell Sydney, which produces about half of the state's petroleum products, would increase by about A$800,000 a year because of the levy, offsetting almost half of the benefit provided by cheaper-priced de-regulated electricity, Ampol said.
Ampol is owned jointly by Pioneer International Ltd and Caltex Australia Ltd.

The NSW government electricity levy, which mining groups see as a fait accompli after passage of the state budget, has been introduced by the government as as adjunct to its de-regulation of the electricity market.
The government has said de-regulation will cut electricity costs to large users by 20 to 40 percent.

The levy would cause an average increase of five percent on previously regulated electricity tariffs, government budget papers said. The levy of 0.55 cents per kilowatt hour (kwh) will apply from July 1 to big electricity customers in NSW.
The levy would increase the annual electricity bill of consumers of more than 40 gigawatt hours a year by A$220,000.
Many members of the Minerals Council would be in this category, the lobby group said.
Large energy users could pay much more than A$1 million extra a year, business groups said.
